stem: What is the BEST way to tell if a CR2032 lithium battery has been discharged?
explanation: The surefire way to check a CR2032 lithium battery is to test its voltage with a multimeter. A CR2032 battery is designed to run at 3 volts, and new ones often ship at about 3.3 volts. Some UEFI/BIOS programs can also monitor the battery voltage, but a direct reading is the reliable test.
whyWrong: A power supply tester checks the PSU's output rails and connectors, not a coin-cell battery.
Windows has no reliable built-in reading of the CMOS battery voltage, so checking within the OS is not a dependable test.
Moving the battery to another motherboard only shows a symptom such as a reset clock and does not measure its charge.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 1

stem: A PC reboots without any warning. You rule out any chance of viruses. When you look at the motherboard, you see that some of the capacitors are swelling and appear distended and out of shape. What should you do?
explanation: Swollen or distended capacitors mean the motherboard is damaged, and they can cause reboots without warning, so replace the motherboard. Replacing individual capacitors would take far too much time and is probably not cost-effective.
whyWrong: A failing hard drive causes read errors or boot failures, and it does not explain swollen capacitors on the motherboard.
Desoldering and replacing capacitors is slow, risky work that is rarely cost-effective compared with a new motherboard.
BIOS settings cannot repair physically damaged capacitors.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 2

stem: A computer you are troubleshooting won’t boot properly. When you power on the computer, the video display is blank, and you hear a series of beeps. What should you do?
options: Consult the vendor documentation for the motherboard.
Remove all memory and replace it.
Unplug the speakers because they are causing a conflict.
explanation: A blank display with a series of beeps is a POST beep code, so consult the motherboard documentation (or the manufacturer's website) to find out what the code means. Beep codes differ by BIOS/UEFI vendor and version. The code points to the failing area, which could be video or RAM.
whyWrong: The computer powers on and runs POST, so the power supply connections are not the first suspect.
Replacing all the memory before you read the beep code is guesswork, and the fault might not be RAM.
Speakers do not cause POST beep codes; the beeps come from the motherboard.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 3

stem: You are troubleshooting a CPU and have already cut power, disconnected the power cable, opened the case, and put on your antistatic strap. What should you do NEXT?
options: Test the motherboard with a multimeter.
explanation: Check the connections next, because loose or unseated connections are a common culprit. Look at the CPU fan connector, the power connectors to the motherboard, and the seating of the CPU cooler before you remove or test parts.
whyWrong: The computer is unplugged and open, so checking the BIOS would mean reassembling it and powering it on first.
Removing the CPU is a more invasive step that comes after the simple connection checks.
Testing the motherboard with a multimeter is an advanced step that comes after the basic connection checks.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 4

stem: What is a possible symptom of a failing CPU?
options: CPU is beyond the recommended voltage range.
BIOS reports low temperatures within the case.
Spyware is installed in the browser.
explanation: If the CPU runs beyond its recommended voltage range for extended periods, it can be a sign of a failing CPU. A computer that won't boot at all points to some other problem, or to a CPU that has already failed.
whyWrong: A computer that will not boot can have many causes, and if the CPU is the cause, it has likely already failed.
Low case temperatures are a good thing, as long as they are not below freezing.
Spyware in the browser is a software security issue that has nothing to do with CPU hardware.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 5

stem: You are repairing a computer that has been used in a warehouse for several years. You suspect a problem with a memory module. What should you do FIRST?
options: Replace the module with a new one.
explanation: A warehouse is often a dirty environment, so first clean the RAM slot with compressed air and clean the memory module with contact cleaner. Clean the dust out of the entire computer as well. Running MemTest86 or another memory diagnostic tool is another good early step.
whyWrong: Replacing the module before you clean and test it may waste a good part when dust is the real problem.
Adding more RAM does not fix a suspected faulty or dirty module.
RAM heat sinks address overheating, and nothing in this scenario points to heat.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 6

stem: You are investigating a computer that is suffering from random shutdowns. You note that the RAM modules are overheating. What is the BEST solution?
options: Install a heat sink on the memory controller.
Install heat sinks on the RAM modules.
Install a heat sink on the chipset.
explanation: The best fix for overheating RAM modules is to install heat sinks on the RAM modules. On older computers the memory controller sits in the northbridge and already has a heat sink; on newer computers it is inside the CPU. An additional case fan might also help the airflow.
whyWrong: The memory controller already has cooling or sits inside the CPU, and it is not the part that is overheating.
More CPU cooling does not target the RAM modules, which are the parts that overheat.
The chipset usually already has a heat sink, and it is not the overheating component.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 7

stem: You just installed new, compatible RAM into a motherboard, but when you boot the computer, it does not recognize the memory. What should you do?
explanation: If you are sure that the RAM is compatible and the system does not recognize it during POST, try flashing the UEFI/BIOS. The RAM might be so new that the motherboard firmware cannot yet identify it, and a firmware update adds that support.
whyWrong: The RAM is known to be compatible, so replacing it is unlikely to help before the firmware is updated.
Upgrading the CPU is costly and does not fix firmware that cannot identify the new memory.
Adding more of the same RAM still leaves the firmware unable to recognize it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 8

stem: You are troubleshooting a computer that won’t power on. You have already checked the AC outlet and the power cord, which appear to be functioning properly. What should you do NEXT?
options: Test the computer with a PSU tester.
Plug the computer into a different outlet.
Check that the RAM is seated correctly.
explanation: Test the computer with a PSU tester, which tells you whether the power supply works properly. You already know that the AC outlet works, so there is no reason to use another outlet. A computer still powers on when the RAM is not seated properly.
whyWrong: The AC outlet already works, so another outlet tells you nothing new.
The computer would still power on if the RAM were not seated properly.
A UPS sits before the power supply in the power flow and will not fix a computer that does not power on.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 9

stem: A computer you are troubleshooting shuts down without warning. After a few minutes, it boots back up, but after running for a short time, it shuts down again. Which of the following components could be the cause? (Select the two best answers.)
explanation: A failing power supply or a failing CPU fan can make the system shut down without warning, and an overheated system boots again after it cools. Check the CPU fan settings and the temperature in the BIOS first, before you open the computer. If those are fine, you most likely need to replace the power supply.
whyWrong: A failing SATA hard drive causes read errors or boot problems, not repeated sudden shutdowns.
RAM faults more often show as errors or crashes than as a power-off that repeats after the system cools.
A failing video card causes display problems rather than shutting down the whole system.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 23: Troubleshooting Motherboards, CPUs, RAM, and Power, Cram Quiz question 10

stem: The power supply fan and case fans spin, but there is no power to other devices. Which of the following is the MOST LIKELY cause of this?
explanation: If the power supply fan and the case fans spin but other devices get no power, the main 24-pin connection from the power supply to the motherboard was most likely not made. The case fans in this case connect straight to the power supply by Molex or SATA power, so they spin while the motherboard, CPU, RAM, and drives get nothing.
whyWrong: A failed boot drive stops the operating system from loading, but the other devices would still get power.
A drive that is not recognized stops the OS from booting, but it does not cut power to other devices.
Failed RAM can cause a boot failure that POST reports, but it does not stop other devices from receiving power.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 10

stem: One of the desktop computers at a customer site is randomly rebooting several times per day. You have checked for overheating issues, but everything seems okay with the case fans, CPU fan, and power supply. What should you check NEXT?
options: Make sure the integrated network adapter has the latest drivers.
Ensure that the storage drive is defragmented.
Check the motherboard for signs of swollen capacitors.
Check the RAM and confirm that it is the right type.
explanation: Check the motherboard for swollen capacitors. A swollen (or distended) capacitor can make the system reboot intermittently, and the capacitor or the entire motherboard then needs to be replaced.
whyWrong: An out-of-date network adapter driver is unlikely to cause random reboots, though keeping drivers current is good practice.
A fragmented drive slows performance but does not make a system reboot.
The wrong type of RAM usually causes a POST failure rather than random reboots.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 11

stem: You are tasked with fixing a laptop that is not booting. You have analyzed the system and can’t see any system lights or display, and you can’t hear any sounds when the power button is pressed. Which of the following should be attempted FIRST when troubleshooting the problem?
options: Boot the system from a flash drive.
Disconnect the AC and the battery and press and hold the power button for several seconds.
Remove storage drives and optical drives, RAM, and USB devices from the laptop.
Connect an external monitor to the laptop to determine if the LCD has failed.
explanation: Disconnect the AC adapter and the battery, then press and hold the power button for several seconds (up to 30 seconds on some models). This discharges the laptop's capacitors and may clear the BIOS, either of which could fix the problem. Afterward, reconnect the battery and AC and continue troubleshooting; you might have to reconfigure the BIOS.
whyWrong: Booting from a flash drive does nothing when the laptop shows no lights, display, or sound at all.
Removing drives, RAM, and USB devices helps in some cases, but not when the laptop shows no sign of power.
An external monitor helps when lights blink but the built-in display is dark; here both displays would likely show nothing.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 31

stem: A computer you are working on randomly reboots. Which of the following should be checked FIRST when troubleshooting the computer? (Select the two best answers.)
explanation: Check the memory and the power supply unit (PSU) first, because both can fail intermittently and cause random reboots. Try reseating and cleaning the RAM, and replace it if necessary. Test the PSU with a PSU tester or a multimeter, and replace it if necessary.
whyWrong: A failed video card stops the display but does not make the computer reboot.
A failed CMOS battery resets the date, time, and BIOS settings rather than causing reboots.
A failed optical drive cannot read discs but does not make the computer reboot.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 35

stem: You just completed a CPU installation. When you turn on the computer, the POST sounds a series of beeps, and the system won’t boot. What is the MOST LIKELY cause?
options: The mouse is not plugged in.
The CPU is not properly seated.
The fan is running too fast.
explanation: Right after a CPU installation, a series of POST beeps and no boot most likely mean that the CPU is not seated properly. The BIOS cannot find the CPU and reports it with beeps. When a computer is being built, poorly seated or incompatible RAM can cause the same result.
whyWrong: A missing mouse does not cause POST beeps, although a missing keyboard can.
POST checks only hardware, so a corrupted operating system does not cause beep codes.
Fan speed is governed by the BIOS/UEFI settings and does not stop the system from booting.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 42

stem: A user calls you and says that their computer won’t boot and that there is a faint smell of something burning. Which tool should be used to identify the problem?
explanation: Use a power supply unit (PSU) tester to check whether the power supply is malfunctioning. If you smell something burning, first turn off the power and disconnect the computer from the AC outlet. A new PSU can give a faint smell during its first 24 to 48 hours, but a computer that suddenly stops working with a burning smell most likely needs a new PSU after testing.
whyWrong: A loopback plug tests a network port, such as a switch port or a computer's RJ45 port.
A cable tester checks network cabling, not power supplies.
An antistatic (ESD) strap protects components from electrostatic discharge; it does not diagnose faults.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 52

stem: You are tasked with fixing a client’s PC that hasn’t booted after the latest test of the building’s backup generator. As you analyze the computer, you notice that once it is powered on, there is no display and there are no beep codes. After 15 seconds, the fans inside the computer start spinning faster and making more noise. The computer was working fine before the test, and you verify that no one has opened the computer. Which of the following is MOST LIKELY the problem?
options: The RAM was damaged by ESD.
The motherboard was damaged by the power test.
The storage drive was erased due to the power test.
The power supply was damaged and is nonfunctional.
explanation: The motherboard was most likely damaged by a surge or spike during the power test, which causes a POST failure and makes the fans behave abnormally. A capacitor might have burst or a circuit burned out, so the motherboard probably needs to be replaced. To protect systems in the future, use a better surge suppressor, a line conditioner, or a UPS.
whyWrong: No one opened the computer, so ESD damage to the RAM is unlikely.
A surge might corrupt the drive's data, but that would not cause the missing display and the fan behavior.
If the power supply were nonfunctional, the fans would not spin at all.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 64

stem: A workstation fails to boot. The POST found an error, and the computer beeps twice. This happens again and again. Which of the following is the MOST LIKELY issue?
explanation: Two beeps often mean a problem with memory, although the meaning depends on the BIOS or UEFI vendor. For example, two beeps on some Dell systems mean no memory was detected, and two short beeps on AMI BIOS systems mean a memory parity error. Read the motherboard documentation to find out what each beep code means.
whyWrong: If the power supply failed, the system would not reach POST at all.
A video adapter failure gives a different beep pattern, such as one long and two short beeps on some BIOS types.
If the CPU fails, the system does not run POST at all.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 67

stem: One of the workstations at your organization was just moved to a new work location in the same building. The new location does not have a surge suppressor. The workstation was working the day before, but today the system will not power up, the fans do not spin, and there are no other signs of activity. Which of the following should you do FIRST?
options: Check the voltage of the PSU with a multimeter.
Check the voltage switch on the PSU.
explanation: First check the power cable connection: when a computer shows no signs of life at all, it is most likely a power problem. Make sure the cable is securely connected to the PSU and to the AC outlet, because the simple checks come first.
whyWrong: Testing the PSU voltage means opening the system, which you do only after the simple external checks.
Swollen capacitors are worth checking later, but the move makes a loose power cable far more likely.
The voltage switch should not have changed when the computer was moved within the same building.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 78

stem: When a user turns on their desktop computer, nothing appears on the screen. They hear three long beeps, followed by three short beeps, and three long beeps. What should you do NEXT?
options: Look up the beep code on the manufacturer's website.
explanation: This system is producing a beep code and not completing the POST process. Different BIOS/UEFI manufacturers use different beep codes. Look up this beep code on the manufacturer's website before replacing any hardware.
whyWrong: Replacing the motherboard before you decode the beeps is a guess that may waste a good part.
The beep pattern may not point to memory at all, so swapping the RAM now is premature.
No hardware should be replaced until the beep code tells you which component failed.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 1

stem: A field technician reports back that the computer they are troubleshooting has exposed distended capacitors. Which component has MOST LIKELY failed?
explanation: Capacitors store energy and are located on the motherboard and inside the power supply. Since the capacitors are exposed, the technician is most likely seeing the problem on the motherboard. The capacitors inside a power supply are hidden by its sealed case.
whyWrong: The power supply's capacitors sit inside its closed metal case, so they would not be exposed to view.
A CPU has no large electrolytic capacitors that can visibly swell.
RAM modules have no large electrolytic capacitors that can visibly swell.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 2

stem: You are troubleshooting a Windows-based desktop computer that is experiencing unexpected shutdowns. Which of the following would be a good NEXT step to resolve the issue? (Choose two.)
options: Replace the motherboard, CPU, and RAM to see if it resolves the problem.
Replace the RAM to see if it resolves the problem.
Reinstall Windows to see if it resolves the problem.
Replace the CPU to see if it resolves the problem.
explanation: Intermittent shutdowns are hard to troubleshoot but are most likely hardware-related. When troubleshooting, always make one change at a time to try to resolve the issue. Replacing the RAM or the CPU to see if it resolves the problem could be a good next step. Narrow down the issue before implementing sweeping solutions.
whyWrong: Replacing three components at once is too many changes, so you would not learn which part was at fault.
Reinstalling Windows is overkill for a problem that is most likely caused by hardware.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 3

stem: When a desktop computer boots up, there is no video on the LED monitor, just a blank screen. The system makes one beep when it powers on, and air is coming out of the case fan. What is the MOST LIKELY cause of the problem?
options: The CPU or RAM has failed.
explanation: When troubleshooting, always question the obvious. In this case, the system beeps once, which is usually a signal from the BIOS that POST completed successfully, and air is coming from the system fan. All of that appears to be normal. Check to see that the monitor is connected properly to the desktop computer and that it's receiving power.
whyWrong: A failed motherboard would not let POST finish with a single success beep.
A failed video card normally produces a POST beep code instead of one normal beep.
A failed CPU or RAM stops POST, so the system would not give the single success beep.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 4

stem: You are training a class of new technicians on troubleshooting motherboard issues. Which of the following are issues MOST LIKELY caused by a failing CMOS battery? (Choose two.)
options: Attempts to boot to the incorrect device
explanation: When the system is powered off, BIOS settings on a motherboard are maintained by the CMOS battery. If the battery fails, the system will likely forget the BIOS time and date settings and the boot order configuration. Replacing the CMOS battery will resolve the issue.
whyWrong: Intermittent device failure points to a failing component or connection, not to lost BIOS settings.
BSOD and pinwheel errors are OS crash screens caused by hardware or driver faults, not by a weak CMOS battery.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 5

stem: A desktop computer is experiencing continuous reboots. It gets to the BIOS screen and then reboots every time. Which two components are MOST LIKELY to cause this problem? (Choose two.)
explanation: Continuous reboots are most likely caused by the motherboard or CPU failing. It's possible it's the RAM, but less likely. The power supply is the least likely cause of the problem in this scenario.
whyWrong: The power supply is the least likely cause here, because the system powers on and reaches the BIOS screen each time.
Failing RAM can cause reboots, but it is a less likely cause than the motherboard or CPU.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 6

stem: A user pushes the power button on their desktop computer but nothing happens. They double-check that it is plugged in and that the wall outlet is working properly. Which components are MOST LIKELY to cause this problem? (Choose two.)
explanation: If the wall outlet is functioning and the power cable is connected properly (always check the obvious), then the most likely culprits are the power supply or the power cord. The motherboard, CPU, and RAM are unlikely to cause a complete power failure in a computer.
whyWrong: A failed motherboard rarely stops the fans and lights from coming on at all.
A failed CPU usually leaves fans spinning with no video, not a completely dead system.
Bad RAM typically causes beep codes or crashes, not a complete lack of power.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 7

stem: A technician who has been troubleshooting a computer tells you that the system is having problems with overheating. Which component is MOST LIKELY to cause this issue?
explanation: The processor runs the hottest of all computer components and is the most likely to overheat. Motherboards and RAM don't generate a lot of heat. Power supplies most often have fans to help dissipate heat, and don't run as hot as CPUs.
whyWrong: A power supply has its own fan to remove heat and does not run as hot as a CPU.
A motherboard does not generate much heat on its own.
RAM modules produce relatively little heat compared to the processor.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 8

stem: When you turn on a desktop computer, you hear a loud squealing noise coming from inside the case. Which components are potential culprits for making the noise? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: Only components with moving parts can make ticking, clicking, or squealing noises. It's probably a fan of some sort (such as the CPU fan or power supply fan), or it could be a conventional hard drive. SSDs, CPUs, and RAM do not have moving parts and therefore could not be causing this problem.
whyWrong: An SSD uses flash memory with no moving parts, so it cannot squeal.
A CPU has no moving parts, so it cannot make a squealing noise.
RAM has no moving parts, so it cannot make a squealing noise.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 10

stem: A user complains of smoke and a foul odor coming from their desktop computer, so they shut it down. Which component is MOST LIKELY causing the problem?
explanation: Smoke and foul odors such as burning smells are not normal for computers. The most likely component causing the problem is the power supply. With the system off, open the computer case (not the power supply case) to examine the inside for possible physical damage.
whyWrong: RAM can fail, but it is rarely the source of smoke and a burning smell.
A CPU can overheat, but it is far less likely than the power supply to give off smoke.
A motherboard can burn, but the power supply is the more common source of smoke and odor.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 11

stem: A Windows user complains that their computer keeps crashing. What is the proprietary crash screen they are MOST LIKELY seeing?
explanation: When Windows-based systems crash, as can happen due to a memory, CPU, or motherboard problem, they will most likely display a Blue Screen of Death (BSOD). The good news is that the BSOD can often provide useful information, such as an error code, to help troubleshoot the problem.
whyWrong: There is no proprietary crash screen called a stop sign.
The spinning pinwheel is the macOS sign of a hung or crashing system, not the Windows one.
A black screen may indicate a crash, but it is not proprietary to one operating system.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 12

stem: A client calls to complain that his computer starts up, but crashes when Windows starts to load. After a brief set of questions, you find out that his nephew upgraded his RAM for him over the weekend and couldn’t get the computer to work right afterward. What could be the problem?
options: There’s nothing wrong. It usually takes a couple of days for RAM to acclimate to the new system.
explanation: Most likely, the nephew disconnected the CPU fan to get at the RAM slots and simply forgot to plug it back in. Without the fan, the CPU overheats quickly under load and the system crashes or shuts down.
whyWrong: Thermal paste breaks down slowly over years, so it does not explain a failure that started right after a RAM upgrade.
A bad CPU cache is unlikely to appear suddenly after a RAM upgrade that did not touch the CPU.
RAM needs no time to acclimate; a fault after an upgrade points to something the installer changed.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 3: CPUs, Chapter Review question 9
note: Older book (220-1101/1102), All-in-One 11e Chapter 3: troubleshooting CPUs (overheating). Mapped to 220-1201/5.1 Overheating.

stem: Darren has installed a new CPU in a client’s computer, but nothing happens when he pushes the power button on the case. The LED on the motherboard is lit up, so he knows the system has power. What could the problem be?
options: He forgot to disconnect the CPU fan.
He forgot to apply thermal paste between the CPU and the heat-sink and fan assembly.
He used an AMD CPU in an Intel motherboard.
He used an Intel CPU in an AMD motherboard.
explanation: The best answer here is that he forgot the thermal paste, though you can also make an argument for a disconnected fan. Without thermal paste, heat does not move from the CPU to the heat sink, so the CPU overheats and the system shuts down almost at once.
whyWrong: The CPU fan should be connected, not disconnected, so forgetting to disconnect it causes no problem.
AMD CPUs do not physically fit Intel motherboard sockets, so this install could not have been done.
Intel CPUs do not physically fit AMD motherboard sockets, so this install could not have been done.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 3: CPUs, Chapter Review question 10
note: Older book (220-1101/1102), All-in-One 11e Chapter 3: installing and troubleshooting CPUs. Mapped to 220-1201/5.1 Overheating.

stem: Steve adds a second 8-GB 288-pin DIMM to his PC, which should bring the total RAM in the system up to 16 GB. The PC has an Intel Core i7 4-GHz processor and four 288-pin DIMM slots on the motherboard. When he turns on the PC, however, only 8 GB of RAM shows up in Windows Settings app. Which of the following is MOST LIKELY to be the problem?
options: Steve failed to seat the RAM properly.
Steve put DDR4 in a DDR3 slot.
The CPU cannot handle 16 GB of RAM.
The motherboard can use only one RAM slot at a time.
explanation: Steve most likely failed to seat the RAM properly. A module that is not fully seated in its slot is not detected, so the system reports only the memory that was already installed.
whyWrong: A 288-pin DIMM cannot be put in a 240-pin DDR3 slot, because the pin count and the notch are different.
A modern Core i7 system easily supports 16 GB of RAM.
A motherboard with four DIMM slots uses all of its populated slots, not just one.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 4: RAM, Chapter Review question 1
note: Older book (220-1101/1102), All-in-One 11e Chapter 4: installing and troubleshooting RAM. No 220-1201 symptom lists missing RAM exactly; mapped to 5.1 Common symptoms.

stem: How does an NMI manifest on a macOS system?
options: NMIs only happen on Windows systems.
explanation: A non-maskable interrupt (NMI) on a macOS system often results in the spinning pinwheel of death. Windows shows the same kind of critical stop as a blue screen of death, and faulty RAM is a common cause of both.
whyWrong: The blue screen of death is the Windows crash screen, not the macOS one.
Interrupt of death is not the name of any crash screen.
NMIs can occur on any system, including macOS and Linux, not just Windows.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 4: RAM, Chapter Review question 5
note: Older book (220-1101/1102), All-in-One 11e Chapter 4: RAM troubleshooting (NMI). Mapped to 220-1201/5.1 Proprietary crash screens.

stem: Gregor installed a third stick of known-good RAM into his Core i7 system, bringing the total amount of RAM up to 12 GB. Within a few days, though, he started having random lockups and reboots, especially when doing memory-intensive tasks such as gaming. What is MOST LIKELY the problem?
options: Gregor installed DDR2 RAM into a DDR3 system.
Gregor installed DDR3 RAM into a DDR4 system.
Gregor installed RAM that didn’t match the speed or quality of the RAM in the system.
Gregor installed RAM that exceeded the speed of the RAM in the system.
explanation: Most likely, Gregor installed RAM that didn't match the speed or quality of the RAM in the system. Mismatched modules can cause random lockups and reboots, especially under memory-intensive loads such as gaming.
whyWrong: DDR2 modules physically do not fit DDR3 slots because the notch is in a different place.
DDR3 modules physically do not fit DDR4 slots because the pin count and notch differ.
Faster RAM normally runs at the speed of the slower installed modules, so it rarely causes crashes.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 4: RAM, Chapter Review question 9
note: Older book (220-1101/1102), All-in-One 11e Chapter 4: RAM troubleshooting. Mapped to 220-1201/5.1 Random shutdown.

stem: Cindy installed a second stick of DDR4 RAM into her Core i5 system, bringing the total system up to 16 GB. Within a short period of time, though, she began experiencing blue screens of death. What could the problem be?
options: The motherboard could only handle 12 GB of RAM.
There is no problem. Windows always does this initially but gets better after crashing a few times.
explanation: If you have no problems with a system and then experience problems after installing something new, chances are the something new is at fault. A faulty RAM stick is a common cause of blue screens of death.
whyWrong: A modern Core i5 motherboard supports far more than 12 GB of RAM.
Dual-channel is a motherboard memory mode, not a type of RAM stick that must be bought.
Windows does not crash as a normal part of adding RAM; repeated blue screens show a fault.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 4: RAM, Chapter Review question 10
note: Older book (220-1101/1102), All-in-One 11e Chapter 4: RAM troubleshooting. Mapped to 220-1201/5.1 Proprietary crash screens.

stem: Every time Jill boots her system, it goes through POST, beeps once, and then loads Windows normally. What is this beep code telling her?
explanation: On almost all systems, a single beep indicates everything is OK. Other beep patterns point to a POST failure, and the motherboard manual lists what each code means.
whyWrong: A bad CPU usually gives no beep or a different beep pattern, not one beep followed by a normal boot.
Bad RAM gives a repeating or specific beep pattern, and the system would not load Windows.
A missing keyboard shows an error or a different beep code, not a single OK beep.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 5: Firmware, Chapter Review question 9

stem: Amanda bought a new system that, right in the middle of an important presentation, gave her a blue screen of death. Now her system won't boot at all, not even to CMOS. After extensive troubleshooting, she determined that the motherboard was at fault and replaced it. Now the system runs fine. What was the MOST LIKELY cause of the problem?
explanation: Although all of the answers are plausible, the best answer here is that her system suffered burn-in failure. A burn-in failure is a component failure that happens early in the life of new hardware, usually within the first days or weeks of use.
whyWrong: Electrostatic discharge is possible but there is no sign of ESD exposure in a new system nobody opened.
A general component failure is plausible, but a failure in a new system fits burn-in failure better.
Replacing the motherboard fixed the system, so the power supply was not the cause.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 6: Motherboards, Chapter Review question 5
note: Older book (220-1101/1102), All-in-One 11e Chapter 6: motherboard troubleshooting. Mapped to 220-1201/5.1 Proprietary crash screens / No power.

stem: Solon has a very buggy computer that keeps locking up at odd moments and rebooting spontaneously. He suspects the motherboard. How should he test it?
options: Check settings and verify good components.
Verify good components and document all testing.
Replace the motherboard first to see if the problems disappear.
Check settings, verify good components, replace components, and document all testing.
explanation: Solon needs to check settings, verify good components, replace components, and document all testing. Working through all of these steps in order isolates the faulty part without guessing.
whyWrong: Checking settings and verifying components is not enough; he must also replace suspect parts and document the tests.
Verifying components and documenting is incomplete without checking settings and replacing parts.
Replacing the motherboard first is costly guesswork that skips simpler checks.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 6: Motherboards, Chapter Review question 7
note: Older book (220-1101/1102), All-in-One 11e Chapter 6: motherboard troubleshooting. Mapped to 220-1201/5.1 Random shutdown.

stem: What can happen if the CPU fan fails to function properly?
options: The CPU may overheat and lead to system instability or shutdown
The CPU’s performance may decrease, causing slower operations
The system may emit a loud noise due to increased fan speed
The CPU may become physically damaged
explanation: If the CPU fan fails, the CPU is not cooled enough and overheats. This causes instability and sudden shutdowns, and the CPU may throttle to protect itself.
whyWrong: The CPU may throttle and slow down, but the main result is overheating that leads to instability or shutdown.
A failed fan stops spinning, so it is silent rather than loud.
Modern CPUs shut down to protect themselves before heat damages them.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 3: Hardware, Objective 3.4 question 11
note: Old objective 220-1101 3.4 (motherboards, CPUs, add-on cards).

stem: When booting up a computer, which component can cause a continuous beeping noise if it is not properly seated?
explanation: Continuous or repeated beeps during POST usually mean a memory problem, such as a RAM module that is not seated correctly. Reseat or replace the module.
whyWrong: A badly seated CPU usually gives no POST or a different beep code.
A power supply fault usually gives no power or random shutdowns, not continuous beeps.
An optical drive problem does not stop POST with beeps.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 3: Hardware, Objective 3.4 question 12
note: Old objective 220-1101 3.4 (motherboards, CPUs, add-on cards).

stem: Which of the following are potential consequences of a CPU running at high temperatures due to worn thermal paste? (Choose two)
options: Reduced CPU performance and slower system response
Increased power consumption and higher energy costs
explanation: When worn thermal paste lets the CPU run hot, the CPU throttles its speed, so the system responds slowly. If the heat gets worse, the system becomes unstable and crashes or shuts down to prevent damage.
whyWrong: Higher temperature does not noticeably raise power use or energy costs.
Modern CPUs throttle and shut down to protect themselves, so a shorter lifespan is not a direct result.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 3: Hardware, Objective 3.4 question 18
note: Book answer marked only "System instability and frequent crashes" for a Choose-two question; corrected to add reduced performance (thermal throttling), which the book explanation also describes. Old objective 220-1101 3.4 (motherboards, CPUs, add-on cards).

stem: Which of the following methods can improve system performance when multiple applications are being used simultaneously?
options: Upgrade the RAM to a higher capacity
Close unnecessary background processes and applications
explanation: More RAM lets several applications stay in memory at the same time without swapping data to the drive. This is the hardware upgrade that best improves performance when many applications run together.
whyWrong: Closing background processes frees some resources, but it does not improve performance as much as more RAM.
A faster SSD improves loading times but does not solve a shortage of memory.
Raising the CPU clock speed adds heat and power use and does not fix a lack of memory.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 3: Hardware, Objective 3.4 question 19
note: Tagged with the sluggish performance symptom; Old objective 220-1101 3.4 (motherboards, CPUs, add-on cards).

stem: A user raises a ticket with the help desk as their desktop computer will not start. On arrival, the computer technician reboots the computer, and it beeps continuously. Which of the following is the problem with the desktop computer?
explanation: Continuous beeps during POST usually mean that the problem is with the RAM modules or the memory controller. Beep codes vary by BIOS vendor, so check the manufacturer’s list to confirm.
whyWrong: A motherboard fault usually gives no beeps or a different beep code, not a continuous beep.
A failed power supply usually gives no beeps at all because the system cannot run POST.
A video adapter fault usually gives a pattern such as 1 long and several short beeps.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.2 question 2
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.2 (motherboards, RAM, CPU, power) = current 5.1.

stem: A computer technician has just installed additional RAM in a desktop computer and it has not been recognized. What should the computer technician do NEXT? (Choose two.)
options: Wear an electromagnetic static wrist strap
explanation: If new memory modules are not detected, check the BIOS/UEFI to see whether it reports the full amount of RAM. If the BIOS does not see them, reseat the memory modules so they are firmly seated in their slots.
whyWrong: An ESD wrist strap protects the modules while you handle them, but it does not make the system detect them.
Rebooting again does not change how the modules are seated, so they will still not be detected.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.2 question 4
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.2 = current 5.1.

stem: A user has complained to the help desk that the time on her computer is inaccurate. She has changed the time twice in the last week, but the computer clock keeps falling behind. The system administrator arrives and confirms that the clock time is inaccurate. What should the system administrator do to rectify the problem?
options: Change the power cable to the computer
Change the complementary metal-oxide semiconductor ( CMOS) battery
Search on the manufacturer’s website to see whether there is an update to the BIOS
explanation: The real-time clock in the chipset keeps the time and date, and the CMOS battery powers it when the computer is off. If the clock keeps losing time, the CMOS battery is failing and needs to be replaced.
whyWrong: The power cable feeds the computer only while it is plugged in; it does not keep the clock running when the system is off.
The PSU does not power the real-time clock when the computer is off, so replacing it will not fix the drift.
A BIOS update does not fix a clock that loses time because its battery is failing.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.2 question 6
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.2 = current 5.1.

stem: A computer technician is carrying out annual maintenance on a desktop computer. When inspecting the motherboard, they notice that one of the capacitors is swollen. They take the computer back to their repair room to replace the capacitor. What is the purpose of capacitors located on the motherboard?
options: The capacitor is used to power the real-time clock
explanation: A capacitor absorbs spikes in the direct current voltage and can temporarily store a charge, which smooths the power to the components. A faulty capacitor becomes swollen, and if it is not replaced, it can burst and damage the computer.
whyWrong: Fans move the air through the case; a capacitor has no part in airflow.
Data is stored in memory and on drives, not in the motherboard capacitors.
The CMOS battery powers the real-time clock, not a capacitor.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.2 question 7
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.2 = current 5.1.

stem: A computer technician is diagnosing a problem with a desktop computer. When they reboot the computer, they hear 1 long beep, followed by 2 short beeps. What does the computer technician diagnose the problem as?
explanation: On many BIOS versions, 1 long beep followed by 2 or 3 short beeps means a video adapter error. A normal POST gives 1 short beep, and beep codes vary by BIOS vendor.
whyWrong: Motherboard faults are usually reported with other beep codes or no beeps at all.
A normal POST gives a single short beep, not 1 long and 2 short beeps.
A failed power supply usually gives no beeps because POST cannot run.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.2 question 9
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.2 = current 5.1.

stem: A computer technician has just been called out to the customer services department as one of the desktop computers has no power. The computer technician pushes the power button and there is no power and they cannot hear any noise from the internal fans. Which of the following should the computer technician carry out when diagnosing the problem? (Choose three.)
options: Check the plug socket is turned on
Plug a lamp into the power socket
explanation: With no power and no fan noise, first check that the wall socket is switched on. Then replace the power cable with a known good cable, and plug a lamp into the socket to confirm that it supplies power.
whyWrong: Memory faults give beep codes after power-on; they do not stop the system from getting power.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.2 question 10
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.2 = current 5.1.

stem: A user has reported to the help desk that they can smell burning coming from their computer. The help desk technician tells the user to immediately turn off the computer and unplug the power from the wall socket. Which of the following could have caused the burning smell? (Select all that apply)
options: The CPU fan is not working
The heatsink is not fitted properly
The fan vents are clogged with dust
explanation: A burning smell comes from components that overheat. A failed CPU fan or a badly fitted heatsink lets the CPU overheat, and an overheating PSU gives off a burning smell. Vents clogged with dust stop the airflow, so the components overheat too.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.2 question 12
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.2 = current 5.1.

stem: Which of the following could cause a computer to perform “sluggishly”?
options: The keyboard is not plugged in
A recent configuration has been made incorrectly
explanation: A computer can perform sluggishly after a configuration change that was made incorrectly. Check recent changes first when performance drops suddenly.
whyWrong: A keyboard that is not plugged in stops typing, but it does not slow down the computer.
A disconnected mouse stops the pointer, but it has no effect on system performance.
A computer with no CPU cannot boot at all, so it cannot run slowly.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.2 question 13
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.2 = current 5.1.

stem: What should you do FIRST to repair a drive that is acting sluggish?
options: Remove the drive and recover the data.
explanation: Attempt to defragment the disk first; if defragmentation is not necessary, Windows lets you know. Then you can move to other options, such as scanning the drive for viruses. Defragmenting applies to magnetic disks, and Windows optimizes SSDs with TRIM instead.
whyWrong: Removing the drive to recover data is drastic for a drive that is only slow, not failing.
Disk Cleanup frees space by deleting temporary files but does not fix the fragmented layout that slows a magnetic disk.
A virus scan is a reasonable later step, but defragmentation is the quick first check for a sluggish drive.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 24: Troubleshooting Storage Drives and RAID Arrays, Cram Quiz question 1

stem: Which of the following are possible symptoms of storage drive failure? (Select the two best answers.)
explanation: System lockups and failing bootup files, or other failing file operations, are possible symptoms of storage drive failure. Other signs include clicking or grinding noises, extended read/write times, and S.M.A.R.T. failure warnings.
whyWrong: Antivirus alerts mean malware was found, which calls for quarantine and a full scan rather than a drive replacement.
Network drives are separate from the local drive, so errors on them point to a network configuration issue.
When the BIOS does not recognize a drive, the usual checks are the cable, the port, and a BIOS update.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 24: Troubleshooting Storage Drives and RAID Arrays, Cram Quiz question 2

stem: You just replaced a SATA drive that you suspect failed. You also replaced the data cable between the drive and the motherboard. When you reboot the computer, you notice that the SATA drive is not recognized by the BIOS. What MOST LIKELY happened to cause this?
options: The drive has not been formatted yet.
The BIOS does not support SATA.
The drive is not jumpered properly.
explanation: Most likely, the SATA port is faulty; it might have been damaged during the upgrade. To test the theory, plug the SATA data cable into another port on the motherboard. A new drive and a new cable that are still not recognized point to the port.
whyWrong: A drive cannot be formatted until the BIOS recognizes it, so formatting is not the cause.
A motherboard with SATA ports has a BIOS that supports SATA drives.
SATA drives do not need jumpers unless they must coexist with older IDE drives, and most current drives have none.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 24: Troubleshooting Storage Drives and RAID Arrays, Cram Quiz question 3

stem: You are troubleshooting a SATA drive that doesn’t function on a PC. When you try it on another computer, it works fine. You suspect a power issue and decide to take voltage readings from the SATA power connector coming from the power supply. Which of the following readings should you find?
explanation: A SATA power connector supplies 3.3 V (orange wire), 5 V (red wire), and 12 V (yellow wire). If any one of these does not test properly, try another SATA power connector from the power supply.
whyWrong: A SATA power connector also carries 3.3 V, so 5 V and 12 V alone is an incomplete reading.
A PC power supply has no 24 V rail; the 24 refers to the pin count of the main motherboard connector.
A SATA power connector also carries 5 V, so 3.3 V and 12 V alone is an incomplete reading.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 24: Troubleshooting Storage Drives and RAID Arrays, Cram Quiz question 4

stem: You are troubleshooting a Windows server that normally boots from a SATA-based RAID 0 array. The message you receive is “missing operating system.” As it turns out, another technician has been updating the BIOS on several of the servers in your organization, including this one. What configured setting needs to be changed? (Select the best answer.)
explanation: When the BIOS was updated, the SATA mode setting probably reverted to AHCI, so the RAID 0 array is ignored and the OS stored on it cannot boot. Change the setting from AHCI back to RAID (or a similar name). RAID 0 stripes the OS across two or more drives, so all the drives must be accessed through RAID for the OS to boot. Back up the BIOS configuration before you update the firmware.
whyWrong: The array in this scenario is RAID 0, so there is no RAID 1 setting to change.
S.M.A.R.T. is the self-monitoring system in HDDs and SSDs and does not control how the drives are presented to the OS.
NVMe is the interface specification for M.2 and PCIe card storage, not the SATA mode setting.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 24: Troubleshooting Storage Drives and RAID Arrays, Cram Quiz question 5

stem: What should you do FIRST if your SATA magnetic disk begins to make loud clicking or grinding noises? (Select the best answer.)
options: Copy the data to another drive.
Replace with a new SATA drive.
explanation: Loud clicking or grinding noises mean the magnetic disk may fail at any moment, so copy the data to another drive right away. Afterward, update the UEFI/BIOS, replace the drive with a new one, and consider a new SATA cable while you are at it.
whyWrong: Replacing the drive before you copy the data risks losing the data on the failing drive.
A firmware update does not stop a mechanical failure and wastes time while the drive may fail.
A SATA power cable does not cause clicking or grinding, which come from the drive's mechanics.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 24: Troubleshooting Storage Drives and RAID Arrays, Cram Quiz question 6

stem: Which are performance measurements for storage drives that measure data transfer capabilities every second? (Select two.)
explanation: Megabytes per second (MB/s) and input/output operations per second (IOPS) are performance measurements that show a drive's data transfer capability each second. Low IOPS or extended read/write times can point to a failing or overloaded drive.
whyWrong: The wmic command shows basic S.M.A.R.T.-based drive information in the Windows Command Prompt; it is a tool, not a measurement.
RAID is an array of storage drives, not a measurement, although you can measure an array's performance.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 24: Troubleshooting Storage Drives and RAID Arrays, Cram Quiz question 7

stem: On your server, two drives of a RAID 5 array have failed. What should you do?
options: Replace one of the drives and run RAID repair.
Replace the failed drives and format the RAID array using the quick option.
Replace one of the failed drives and repair the RAID array using system utilities.
Replace the failed drives and restore the data from tape backup to the repaired RAID array.
explanation: When two drives of a RAID 5 array fail, the whole array fails, because RAID 5 can rebuild from parity only when one drive fails. Replace both failed drives and restore all the data from backup, such as tape or the cloud.
whyWrong: Replacing only one drive leaves the array with two missing members, which RAID 5 parity cannot rebuild.
A quick format gives an empty array, but without restoring from backup, all the data is still lost.
System utilities can repair a RAID 5 array only when a single drive has failed.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 28

stem: You replace a failed storage drive with a new one. You then boot to a special preinstallation environment media so that you can install a custom operating system build that is meant for deployment to the network. The storage drive is recognized in the UEFI/BIOS, but once you have booted to the preinstallation environment, the storage drive is not recognized, the process fails, and the drive can’t be imaged. Which of the following statements best describes the MOST LIKELY problem?
options: The PC’s power supply cannot provide enough power for the new drive.
The boot media has failed and needs to be replaced.
The storage drive has not been partitioned correctly.
The storage drive must be configured in the UEFI/BIOS.
explanation: The storage drive has most likely not been partitioned correctly. The preinstallation environment (PE), often on a USB flash drive or boot disc, boots the system and partitions the drive so that the image can be installed over the network. If the drive is not partitioned properly, the process fails because the image expects a specific partition.
whyWrong: If the PSU could not power the drive, the drive would not appear in the UEFI/BIOS.
The PE booted successfully, so the boot media has not failed.
Drives rarely need configuring in the UEFI/BIOS unless they belong to a RAID array, and this drive is already recognized there.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 75

stem: A technician powers on a server and receives the error message “RAID Array Not Found.” The system previously booted from a RAID 0 configuration. Which of the following is the MOST LIKELY cause of this issue?
options: The RAID controller firmware was corrupted or reset to default.
One of the drives was accidentally reformatted during maintenance.
The system was infected with ransomware that deleted the array.
The boot order in Windows Disk Management is incorrect.
explanation: A “RAID Array Not Found” error after POST is a common sign that the RAID configuration is missing, disabled, or corrupted. The most likely cause is that RAID was disabled or reset in the BIOS, for example when a technician flashes or resets the BIOS and the SATA mode reverts from RAID to AHCI. The RAID utility then does not load at boot, and the system sees the drives as individual, nonbootable disks.
whyWrong: Reformatting one drive of a RAID 0 array loses data, but the array would still be detected, though broken.
Ransomware usually encrypts data and leaves ransom notes; it does not cause hardware-level boot errors.
Windows Disk Management cannot control the boot order at the hardware level or affect whether the array is detected at POST.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 84

stem: You turn on a desktop computer and it fails to boot. You hear a rhythmic ticking coming from inside the case. What is MOST LIKELY the problem?
explanation: Only components with moving parts can make ticking or clicking noises. This question assumes that the hard drive is an HDD and not an SSD, but none of the other components would make a ticking noise. A rhythmic clicking from a magnetic drive often means the read/write heads are failing.
whyWrong: A motherboard has no moving parts, so it cannot make a rhythmic ticking sound.
A CPU has no moving parts, so it cannot make a rhythmic ticking sound.
RAM has no moving parts, so it cannot make a rhythmic ticking sound.
A bomb is a joke choice; a ticking noise inside a PC case points to a mechanical drive.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 9

stem: You turn on a laptop computer and the hard drive is not recognized. Where should you go to troubleshoot the issue?
explanation: If the hard drive is not recognized, the BIOS/UEFI is the place to check. It shows whether the system detects the drive at all and whether the drive is enabled and in the boot order.
whyWrong: Most systems do not include built-in S.M.A.R.T. diagnostics, and S.M.A.R.T. reports on drives that are already detected.
Windows Device Manager cannot be reached when the drive that holds the OS is not recognized.
There is no tool called a boot sector manager.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 17

stem: You are troubleshooting a server and discover that one of the hard drives in the RAID 0 array has failed. Which statement is true?
options: You need to replace the failed drive, but the data is okay because the drive is configured as a mirror.
You need to replace the failed drive, but the data is okay because the drive is configured as a disk stripe with parity.
You need to replace the failed drive, and the data on the array is lost.
You do not need to replace the failed drive; the system will function normally.
explanation: A RAID 0 array is also known as disk striping. RAID 0 actually decreases your fault tolerance versus one hard drive because there are more points of failure. You need to replace the drive, and hopefully you had it backed up so that you can restore the data.
whyWrong: A mirror is RAID 1; a RAID 0 array has no redundant copy of the data.
Disk striping with parity is RAID 5; RAID 0 stores no parity information.
RAID 0 has no fault tolerance, so the array cannot keep working after a drive fails.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 1 – Chapter 12: Core Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 19

stem: What is a potential cause of a clicking noise when booting up a computer?
explanation: A clicking noise during startup often means a failing hard drive with a mechanical fault, such as a bad read/write head. Back up the data at once and replace the drive.
whyWrong: An overheating CPU causes shutdowns or slow performance, not clicking.
A loose power cable causes loss of power, not a clicking noise.
A failing graphics card causes display problems, not clicking.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 3: Hardware, Objective 3.4 question 8
note: Old objective 220-1101 3.4 (motherboards, CPUs, add-on cards).

stem: What is a potential consequence of operating a disk infrastructure in a degraded state?
explanation: A degraded RAID array has lost one or more disks and keeps running on the remaining disks with reduced or no redundancy. If another disk fails before the faulty one is replaced, data can be lost.
whyWrong: A degraded array does not use less power in any useful way.
A degraded array usually runs slower, because it must rebuild data from parity or the remaining disks.
A degraded state reduces data protection; it does not improve security.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 3: Hardware, Objective 3.4 question 10
note: Old objective 220-1101 3.4 (motherboards, CPUs, add-on cards).

stem: Which of the following would produce a grinding noise? ( Choose two)
options: A problem with the carriage mechanism of an inkjet printer
A problem with the hard drive
explanation: On an inkjet printer, a grinding noise indicates a fault in the carriage mechanism. On a hard drive, any grinding or clicking indicates a mechanical problem, while a healthy hard drive makes only a low noise.
whyWrong: RAM has no moving parts, so it cannot make a grinding noise.
A motherboard has no moving parts that grind; its faults show as beep codes or no POST.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.2 question 14
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.2. Book option said 'a toner cartridge on an inkjet printer'; inkjets use ink cartridges, so the option names the carriage mechanism, as the book explanation does.

stem: A system administrator receives an alert from their mail server that one of the disks has failed. They log in to the server and can see only four out of their five disks. They have a hardware RAID 5 solution and therefore they can hot-swap the failed disk. What risk, if any, will the system administrator encounter when replacing the failed disk?
options: RAID 5 is redundant and there is no risk at all
Pull the disks out one at a time and look for the SCSI ID of the failed disk
Look on the RAID array and look for the disk with the red light
If you remove a healthy disk, you will lose all your data
explanation: RAID 5 keeps working when only one drive fails. If you remove a healthy disk by mistake, the RAID controller sees a two-drive failure and you lose all the data, so identify the failed disk before you pull it.
whyWrong: RAID 5 survives one failed disk, but removing a second (healthy) disk while it is degraded destroys the array.
Pulling disks out one at a time to find the failed one would remove a healthy disk and cause data loss.
The red status light shows which disk failed, but it does not describe the risk of the replacement.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.3 question 2
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.3 = current 5.2.

stem: A user boots up their computer and receives a S.M.A.R.T. error that says a hard disk failure is imminent. What should the user do NEXT?
options: Go to Disk Management and format the disk to get rid of errors
Swap out the disk for a new disk
explanation: S.M.A.R.T. (Self-Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Technology) monitors the health of hard drives. When it reports that a failure is imminent, the disk cannot be repaired: back up the data and replace the disk.
whyWrong: Running another S.M.A.R.T. self-test only repeats the warning; the disk is already reported as failing.
Formatting does not repair a failing disk and destroys the data on it.
Disabling S.M.A.R.T. hides the warnings but the disk will still fail.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.3 question 3
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.3 = current 5.2. The book stem showed the S.M.A.R.T. error in a figure; the stem now states it in words, from the book explanation.

stem: A computer technician is trying to find out why a computer cannot boot. They take out the hard disk and connect it to a computer with recovery software. They are able to see the data. What should the computer technician do NEXT?
options: Put the disk back into the computer and boot from it
Format the disk using Disk Management
Put the disk back into the computer and then install the recovery software
explanation: If a computer cannot boot from a hard drive but recovery software can still read the data, back up the data at once, because the disk could fail at any time. Being able to read the data does not mean the disk is bootable.
whyWrong: Recovery software can read the data, but that does not make the disk bootable again.
Formatting erases the data, and a failing disk may not work properly after it.
Installing recovery software on the disk does not make it bootable and risks overwriting data.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.3 question 4
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.3 = current 5.2.

stem: A user’s computer fails to boot up and they notice the hard drive LED is a solid orange. Which of the following could be causing this issue?
options: The computer has a memory problem
There is a hardware problem with the hard disk drive
The computer has a processor problem
SMART monitoring has been disabled, causing the computer to freeze
explanation: A solid orange (amber) drive LED usually indicates a hardware or driver fault with the hard disk drive. Check the drive vendor’s LED codes to confirm the fault.
whyWrong: A memory problem usually gives beep codes during POST, not an orange drive LED.
A processor fault stops the system before POST and does not change the drive status light.
Disabling S.M.A.R.T. only removes early warnings; it does not freeze the computer or light the drive LED.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.3 question 7
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.3 = current 5.2.

stem: A computer technician runs a performance test against a computer’s hard drive. The test reveals that the disk is suffering from extended read/write times. What should the technician do NEXT?
options: Run the system diagnostic program that was supplied with the computer
Swap out the disk with a new disk
explanation: First run the system diagnostic program that was supplied with the computer, which should reveal the cause of the extended read/write times. Swapping the disk is premature, because the diagnostic test may find only a minor error.
whyWrong: A S.M.A.R.T. self-test is useful after the system diagnostics, so you are warned of an imminent disk failure.
Replacing the disk is premature until a diagnostic test shows that the disk is failing.
Disabling S.M.A.R.T. removes the warnings of disk failure and never helps.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.3 question 8
note: Book answer C (swap out the disk) corrected: the book explanation and the facts say to run the supplied system diagnostics first. Old 220-1101 objective 5.3 = current 5.2.

stem: A computer that is configured with RAID 5 receives an alert that the array is in a degraded state. Which of the following is causing this error and how does it affect the data? (Choose two.)
options: One of the disks in the RAID 5 set needs to be formatted to NTFS
One of the disks in the RAID 5 set has failed
The data is no longer available
explanation: A degraded alert means that one of the disks in the RAID 5 set has failed. RAID 5 survives one failed disk, so the data is still available, but back it up and replace the disk at once.
whyWrong: The file system has nothing to do with a degraded array, and a failed disk cannot be formatted.
RAID 5 parity keeps the data available after one disk fails.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.3 question 9
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.3 = current 5.2.

stem: A computer technician boots up a computer and gets the error message “missing operating system.” Which of the following is causing this error?
options: There is a disk missing from a RAID set
The computer is having a Windows update
The disk with the operating system has failed
explanation: When the disk that holds the operating system fails or cannot be read, the computer reports a “missing operating system” or bootable device not found error. Check the boot order and the drive connection, then test the drive.
whyWrong: A disk missing from a RAID set makes the array report a degraded state, not a missing operating system.
A Windows update boots the computer and then shows that it is updating.
A failing CMOS battery makes the date and time wrong; it does not remove the operating system.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.3 question 10
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.3 = current 5.2.

stem: How can you tell if a storage device’s performance is degrading?
options: There will be a solid orange light
There will be a flashing green light
explanation: To check whether a storage device’s performance is degrading, measure its input/output operations per second (IOPS) and compare them with the manufacturer’s baseline. Low IOPS show that the device is slowing down.
whyWrong: A solid orange light indicates a drive fault, not a gradual drop in performance.
Disk Management shows volumes and their status but does not measure drive performance.
A flashing green light shows normal drive activity, not a measure of its performance.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 5: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting, Objective 5.3 question 11
note: Old 220-1101 objective 5.3 = current 5.2.

stem: A user set the resolution in Windows too high, resulting in a scrambled, distorted display. What should you do to fix the problem? (Select the best answer.)
explanation: Boot into a low-resolution mode, called Enable low-resolution video in Windows, and then set a resolution that the display supports. Safe Mode is another valid option, but it loads a minimal set of drivers and has no Internet access. Pressing the monitor toggle key might show the screen on a secondary monitor for a while, but it does not solve the root cause.
whyWrong: The driver is not the fault here, and you cannot easily work in Windows while the display is scrambled.
The monitor toggle key might send the image to another display, but it leaves the wrong resolution in place.
Loose video connections do not explain a distortion that started right after the resolution was set too high.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 25: Troubleshooting Video Issues, Cram Quiz question 1

stem: You are troubleshooting a video issue. Which utility should you use?
explanation: Use DxDiag (the DirectX Diagnostic Tool) to troubleshoot video issues. It shows the display adapter, the driver version, and the DirectX features, and it can test them.
whyWrong: Regedit is used for advanced configuration in the registry, not for video diagnostics.
Msconfig changes how the system boots and enables or disables services.
Task Manager shows the computer's performance and the running applications and processes.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 25: Troubleshooting Video Issues, Cram Quiz question 2

stem: You receive a basic computer that has a broken onboard DVI connector. What should you attempt FIRST?
explanation: Try installing a video card first to see if the system still works. Unless it is a specialized system, a video card costs less than a motherboard and takes far less time to install.
whyWrong: Replacing the motherboard costs more and takes longer than adding a video card.
PC techs usually do not replace soldered connectors, so this step belongs further down the list.
An adapter cannot help when the DVI port itself is broken.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 25: Troubleshooting Video Issues, Cram Quiz question 3

stem: You just replaced a video card in a PC with another card from a different manufacturer. However, the driver installation does not complete. What should you do FIRST?
options: Locate the latest version of the driver.
explanation: If the driver installation does not complete, roll back the driver; you might have tried to install the incorrect driver. After the rollback, find the correct latest version of the driver on the manufacturer's website. Reinstall the original video card only temporarily if you cannot find a proper solution right away.
whyWrong: Installing the same driver again will most likely give the same result.
Find the correct latest driver after you roll back the failed installation, not before.
Going back to the original card is a temporary fallback for when no proper solution can be found right away.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 25: Troubleshooting Video Issues, Cram Quiz question 4

stem: You are helping a project manager with a presentation using a laptop that feeds video to a projector. During your tests, the projector’s image begins to flicker. The laptop’s display does not have any problems. You attempt to change the resolution on the laptop, but the issue continues. Which of the following should you do NEXT?
options: Check the connectivity of the video cable.
Change the aspect ratio of the laptop.
Check the connectivity of the power cable.
explanation: Check the connectivity of the video cable; a loose cable or a low-quality cable can make the projected image flicker. Screen flicker is more common with older VGA cables, but it can happen with almost any connection. Always check the basics first: connectivity, power, and so on.
whyWrong: Projector settings are unlikely to cause flicker, and the cable should be checked before them.
Most laptops cannot change the aspect ratio by itself, and the resolution change already affected it.
A loose power cable would more likely make the projector power off and on than make the image flicker.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 25: Troubleshooting Video Issues, Cram Quiz question 5

stem: A user needs to transmit video and audio to an external monitor. Which of the following technologies allows this? (Select two.)
explanation: HDMI and DisplayPort connections and cables can transmit both video and audio. USB-C can also carry video, audio, and data.
whyWrong: An onscreen display (OSD) is the monitor's control menu for settings such as position, contrast, and brightness, not a connection.
DVI carries video only, not audio.
VGA is an analog connection that carries video only.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 25: Troubleshooting Video Issues, Cram Quiz question 6

stem: What are common causes of distorted images or misaligned visuals being displayed on a monitor? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Distorted images, such as stretched, compressed, or misaligned visuals, often come from resolution mismatches or improper monitor calibration. For example, a 16:9 widescreen resolution on a standard 4:3 monitor can make images look stretched or squished. Make sure the resolution and aspect ratio match the monitor's specifications.
whyWrong: A burned-out bulb is a projector problem, and it gives no light at all rather than a distorted image.
An incorrect input source gives no signal and a black screen rather than a distorted image.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 25: Troubleshooting Video Issues, Cram Quiz question 7

stem: A monitor’s onscreen display (OSD) indicates that the proper video source has been selected, yet no image is displayed. Which of the following are the MOST LIKELY causes? (Select the two best answers.)
options: The monitor’s brightness setting is too low.
There is no device sending video.
The source cable has been disconnected.
